claim: Lymphoblastoid cell lines (LCLs) from six individuals were reprogrammed into induced pluripotent stem cells (IPSCs).
source: We have reprogrammed lymphoblastoid cell lines (LCLs) from six individuals into induced pluripotent stem cells (IPSCs), which were further differentiated into cardiomyocytes (CMs) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript directly states this experimental procedure in the Results section.

claim: IPSCs were further differentiated into cardiomyocytes (CMs).
source: We have reprogrammed lymphoblastoid cell lines (LCLs) from six individuals into induced pluripotent stem cells (IPSCs), which were further differentiated into cardiomyocytes (CMs) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript directly states this experimental procedure in the Results section.

claim: Each batch consisted of the same cell type from three individuals, with 28 treatments and two controls.
source: Each batch consisted of the same cell type from three individuals, with 28 treatments and two controls.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the experimental design.

claim: Each experiment was performed in duplicate for a total of 12 batches.
source: Each experiment was performed in duplicate for a total of 12 batches.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the experimental design.

claim: CM cellular metabolism was shifted from fetal-associated glycolysis to adult-associated aerobic respiration by replacing cell culture media with galactose-containing media on day 20.
source: In order to shift CM cellular metabolism from fetal-associated glycolysis to adult-associated aerobic respiration, we replaced the cell culture media with galactose-containing media on day 20 (Rana et al., 2012; Ward and Gilad, 2019).
evidence: The manuscript describes this procedure and cites previous work supporting this approach.

claim: CM culture purities ranged from 44.9 to 95%.
source: Purities ranged from 44.9 to 95% (LABEL:SuppTable14).
evidence: The manuscript reports measured purity values.

claim: Principal components analysis on gene expression reveals three distinct clusters corresponding to the three cell types.
source: Principal components analysis on gene expression reveals three distinct clusters corresponding to the three cell types (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references a figure showing the PCA results.

claim: TNNT2 showed high expression in CM samples and low expression in IPSC and LCL samples.
source: including TNNT2, which, as expected, showed high expression in CM samples and low expression in IPSC and LCL samples (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The manuscript reports this observation and references a figure.

claim: Between 53 (insulin in IPSCs) and 21,593 (copper in LCLs) differentially expressed genes (DEGs; FDR < 10%) out of 58,300 genes were identified.
source: We found between 53 (insulin in IPSCs) and 21,593 (copper in LCLs) differentially expressed genes (DEGs; FDR < 10%) out of 58,300 genes.
evidence: The manuscript reports the range of DEGs identified.

claim: Glucose catabolic pathways were enriched (FDR = 0.40%) in genes upregulated in response to insulin in CMs relative to all genes expressed in CMs.
source: For example, as expected glucose catabolic pathways were enriched (FDR = 0.40%) in genes upregulated in response to insulin in CMs relative to all genes expressed in CMs (LABEL:SuppTable2).
evidence: The manuscript reports this enrichment analysis result.

claim: Divalent metal ion transport (FDR = 1.8%) and transition metal ion transport (FDR = 2.8%) were enriched in genes upregulated in response to copper in LCLs.
source: Also, divalent metal ion transport (FDR = 1.8%) and transition metal ion transport (FDR = 2.8%) were enriched in genes upregulated in response to copper in LCLs.
evidence: The manuscript reports this enrichment analysis result.

claim: 4835 genes show evidence of cell type × treatment interaction effects on gene expression (FDR < 10%).
source: When we considered a model with all cell types together, we identified 4835 genes that show evidence of cell type × treatment interaction effects on gene expression as measured by a likelihood ratio test in DESeq2 (FDR < 10%, LABEL:SuppTable17, see Materials and methods Equation 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports this statistical analysis result.

claim: 96% of differentially expressed genes in CMs in response to treatment with insulin are not differentially expressed in LCLs or IPSCs.
source: Interestingly, 96% of differentially expressed genes in CMs in response to treatment with insulin are not differentially expressed in LCLs or IPSCs.
evidence: The manuscript reports this comparison across cell types.

claim: 22,334,519 unique introns were identified, corresponding to 101,450 different transcripts and 14,066 different genes among all cell types and treatment exposures.
source: We identified 22,334,519 unique introns, corresponding to 101,450 different transcripts and 14,066 different genes among all cell types and treatment exposures.
evidence: The manuscript reports these counts from splicing analysis.

claim: Between 9 (insulin in IPSCs) and 4106 (copper in LCLs) differentially spliced genes (DSGs; FDR < 10%) were found between treatment and control in each cell type.
source: We found between 9 (insulin in IPSCs) and 4106 (copper in LCLs) differentially spliced genes (DSGs; FDR < 10%) between treatment and control in each cell type.
evidence: The manuscript reports the range of DSGs identified.

claim: 10 out of 36 environments (∼29%) show a consistent shift (FDR < 10%) in one direction of intron splicing.
source: We identified 10 out of 36 environments (∼29%) that show a consistent shift (FDR < 10%) in one direction of intron splicing (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports this statistical finding and references a figure.

claim: On average 12.6% of the DSGs were found to be also DEGs in a given condition.
source: On average 12.6% of the DSGs were found to be also DEGs in a given condition (Figure 1D).
evidence: The manuscript reports this overlap percentage.

claim: Cell type identity has the strongest effect on both gene expression and splicing variance across samples for most genes (variance explained median value 74% and 70%, respectively).
source: As expected, cell type identity has the strongest effect on both gene expression and splicing variance across samples for most genes (variance explained median value 74% and 70%, respectively, which is consistently bigger than the batch effect), with a relatively small contribution from the individual and treatment (Figure 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports variance partitioning results.

claim: The contribution of the individual is largest in CMs (55% gene expression, 45% splicing), followed by LCLs (36% gene expression, 28% splicing) and IPSCs (28% gene expression, 20% splicing).
source: For example the contribution of the individual is largest in CMs (55% gene expression, 45% splicing), followed by LCLs (36% gene expression, 28% splicing) and IPSCs (28% gene expression, 20% splicing), similar to what was shown previously for gene expression (Banovich et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript reports variance partitioning results and cites previous work.

claim: Treatment explained the greatest percentage of variance in LCLs (22% gene expression, 12% splicing), followed by IPSCs (11% gene expression, 6% splicing), then CMs (4% gene expression, 2% splicing).
source: Treatment explained the greatest percentage of variance in LCLs (22% gene expression, 12% splicing), followed by IPSCs (11% gene expression, 6% splicing), then CMs (4% gene expression, 2% splicing).
evidence: The manuscript reports variance partitioning results.

claim: Treatment (marginal and interaction with individual) explained at least half of the variance for 64% of the genes.
source: When we focused on the variance explained by measured variables (plate, treatment, individual and their interaction), we found that treatment (marginal and interaction with individual) explained at least half of the variance for 64% of the genes.
evidence: The manuscript reports this variance analysis result.

claim: 282,278 unique SNPs in 22,397 genes were quantified for ASE.
source: In total, we quantified ASE at 282,278 unique SNPs in 22,397 genes.
evidence: The manuscript reports the total number of SNPs and genes analyzed.

claim: The number of SNPs with ASE across treatments within each cell type ranges from 612 to 1052 for LCLs, 607-1342 for IPSCs, and 812-1310 for CMs.
source: The number of SNPs with ASE across treatments within each cell type ranges from 612 to 1052 for LCLs, 607-1342 for IPSCs, and 812-1310 for CMs (Figure 3A).
evidence: The manuscript reports these ranges and references a figure.

claim: 15,497 (∼23%) SNPs show evidence of ASE in any condition (ANOVA test, FDR < 10%).
source: We first identified 15,497 (∼23%) SNPs that show evidence of ASE in any condition (ANOVA test Equations 3 and 4, FDR < 10%, LABEL:SuppTable9), corresponding to 5640 genes.
evidence: The manuscript reports this statistical analysis result.

claim: High correlation of ASE between replicates was observed (Spearman's correlation median=0.66).
source: Reassuringly, we observed high correlation of ASE between replicates (i.e. same individual, treatment, and cell type in different batches; Spearman's correlation median=0.66), which confirms that technical effects have a limited impact and that ASE measurements are reproducible (Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript reports this correlation analysis result.

claim: 7866 instances of cell type cASE (5452 unique SNPs, FDR < 10%) were identified, corresponding to gene × cell type interactions.
source: We identified 7866 instances of cell type cASE (5452 unique SNPs, FDR < 10%), corresponding to gene × cell type interactions; 1409 instances of treatment cASE (1102 unique SNPs, FDR 10%), corresponding to gene × treatment interactions; and 929 instances of cell type × treatment cASE (715 unique SNPs, FDR < 10%), corresponding to gene × cell type × treatment interactions (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: The manuscript reports these statistical analysis results.

claim: 1409 instances of treatment cASE (1102 unique SNPs, FDR 10%) were identified, corresponding to gene × treatment interactions.
source: We identified 7866 instances of cell type cASE (5452 unique SNPs, FDR < 10%), corresponding to gene × cell type interactions; 1409 instances of treatment cASE (1102 unique SNPs, FDR 10%), corresponding to gene × treatment interactions; and 929 instances of cell type × treatment cASE (715 unique SNPs, FDR < 10%), corresponding to gene × cell type × treatment interactions (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: The manuscript reports these statistical analysis results.

claim: 929 instances of cell type × treatment cASE (715 unique SNPs, FDR < 10%) were identified, corresponding to gene × cell type × treatment interactions.
source: We identified 7866 instances of cell type cASE (5452 unique SNPs, FDR < 10%), corresponding to gene × cell type interactions; 1409 instances of treatment cASE (1102 unique SNPs, FDR 10%), corresponding to gene × treatment interactions; and 929 instances of cell type × treatment cASE (715 unique SNPs, FDR < 10%), corresponding to gene × cell type × treatment interactions (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: The manuscript reports these statistical analysis results.

claim: 3033 genes with ASE were identified in CMs.
source: In CMs, we identified 3033 genes with ASE.
evidence: The manuscript reports this count.

claim: 50% (1519) of CM ASE genes were eGenes in left ventricle from GTEx.
source: Of these genes, 50% (1519) and 52% (1619) were eGenes in left ventricle and atrial appendage from GTEx, respectively.
evidence: The manuscript reports this overlap analysis result.

claim: 52% (1619) of CM ASE genes were eGenes in atrial appendage from GTEx.
source: Of these genes, 50% (1519) and 52% (1619) were eGenes in left ventricle and atrial appendage from GTEx, respectively.
evidence: The manuscript reports this overlap analysis result.

claim: Treatment cASE genes in CMs were not significantly enriched in GTEx left ventricle or atrial appendage eGenes (odds ratio = 1.02, 0.95).
source: Interestingly, treatment cASE genes in CMs were not significantly enriched in either tissue (odds ratio = 1.02, 0.95).
evidence: The manuscript reports this enrichment analysis result.

claim: Most treatment cASE SNPs were specific to one treatment (80.5%).
source: Most treatment cASE SNPs were specific to one treatment (80.5%, Figure 3—figure supplement 2), so there was little sharing between treatments (Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports this percentage and references figures.

claim: Both ASE and cASE SNPs were found to be significantly enriched in 5' and 3' UTRs, and among variants classified as missense or altering a stop codon (FDR < 10%).
source: When we considered all variants that could be tested for ASE, both ASE and cASE SNPs were found to be significantly enriched in 5' and 3' UTRs, and among variants classified as missense or altering a stop codon (FDR < 10%, Fisher's exact test; Figure 3G).
evidence: The manuscript reports this enrichment analysis result.

claim: SNPs located within upstream/downstream transcript and genic regions, within introns and in splicing sites were found to be significantly depleted in ASE/cASE SNPs.
source: On the contrary, SNPs located within upstream/downstream transcript and genic regions, within introns and in splicing sites were found to be significantly depleted in ASE/cASE SNPs.
evidence: The manuscript reports this enrichment analysis result.

claim: Heart rate was the only cardiovascular trait with a significant overlap with CM-specific cASE, compared to the average overlap with other cardiovascular traits (FDR < 10%).
source: Heart rate was the only trait with a significant overlap with CM-specific cASE, compared to the average overlap with other cardiovascular traits (FDR < 10%).
evidence: The manuscript reports this trait enrichment analysis result.

claim: Genes associated with low birthweight are enriched for genes that have caffeine cASE.
source: For example, genes associated with low birthweight are enriched for genes that have caffeine cASE (Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript reports this enrichment finding and references a figure.

claim: For the 428 genes associated with coronary artery disease (CAD), cASE for metal treatments have the greatest overlap, with cadmium and copper each having five cASE genes associated with CAD, and zinc having three.
source: For the 428 genes associated with coronary artery disease (CAD), cASE for metal treatments have the greatest overlap, with cadmium and copper each having five cASE genes associated with CAD, and zinc having three (Figure 4C).
evidence: The manuscript reports this overlap analysis result.

claim: Cadmium causes endothelial dysfunction and promotes atherosclerosis.
source: Interestingly, cadmium causes endothelial dysfunction and promotes atherosclerosis (Messner et al., 2009), while copper deficiency has been linked to the development of CAD (DiNicolantonio et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work supporting this claim.

claim: Copper deficiency has been linked to the development of CAD.
source: Interestingly, cadmium causes endothelial dysfunction and promotes atherosclerosis (Messner et al., 2009), while copper deficiency has been linked to the development of CAD (DiNicolantonio et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work supporting this claim.

claim: FAM213A (also known as PRXL2A) is involved in redox regulation.
source: FAM213A (also known as PRXL2A), which is involved in redox regulation (Guo et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2010) is shared as treatment cASE for cadmium and copper, in addition to being treatment cASE for nicotine.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work supporting this claim.

claim: Ten genes from an atrial fibrillation GWAS displayed treatment cASE in at least one condition, for a total of 21 gene-cASE condition pairs.
source: Ten of these genes displayed treatment cASE in at least one condition, for a total of 21 gene-cASE condition pairs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, LABEL:SuppTable12).
evidence: The manuscript reports this overlap analysis result.

claim: Three genes in OMIM with gene × treatment interactions in CMs are known to cause Mendelian forms of heart disease: PSMA6, AARS2, DSC2.
source: In CMs, we found three genes in OMIM (Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man) (Hamosh et al., 2005) with gene × treatment interactions that are known to cause Mendelian forms of heart disease: PSMA6, AARS2, DSC2.
evidence: The manuscript reports this finding and cites OMIM.

claim: AARS2 displayed cASE in response to nicotine and mutations in this gene cause Combined Oxidative Phosphorylation Deficiency 8, which manifests as fatal infantile hypertrophic mitochondrial cardiomyopathy.
source: AARS2 displayed cASE in response to nicotine and mutations in this gene cause Combined Oxidative Phosphorylation Deficiency 8, which manifests as fatal infantile hypertrophic mitochondrial cardiomyopathy (Figure 4D).
evidence: The manuscript reports this finding and references a figure.

claim: DSC2 displayed cASE in response to copper and mutations in this gene cause Arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia 11.
source: DSC2, instead, displayed cASE in response to copper and mutations in this gene cause Arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia 11 (Figure 4E).
evidence: The manuscript reports this finding and references a figure.

claim: CM cell type cASE was significantly enriched for diastolic blood pressure, autoimmune disease, and height.
source: CM cell type cASE was significantly enriched for diastolic blood pressure, autoimmune disease, and height.
evidence: The manuscript reports this heritability partitioning result.

claim: Diastolic blood pressure was enriched for vitamin A, systolic blood pressure was enriched for vitamin A, copper, and zinc.
source: Diastolic blood pressure was enriched for vitamin A, systolic blood pressure was enriched for vitamin A, copper, and zinc.
evidence: The manuscript reports this heritability partitioning result.

claim: Respiratory disease was enriched for caffeine, and smoking status for selenium.
source: Respiratory disease was enriched for caffeine, and smoking status for selenium.
evidence: The manuscript reports this heritability partitioning result.

claim: When considering all cell types together, the greatest amount of explainable variance in ASE was captured by the cell type.
source: When considering all cell types together, the greatest amount of explainable variance in ASE was captured by the cell type (Figure 5A, LABEL:SuppTableMixed_All), similar to the results explaining variability in gene expression (Figure 3A).
evidence: The manuscript reports this variance partitioning result.

claim: 17.5%, 16.6%, and 16.8% of variance (median) in ASE was attributed to treatment effects in CMs, IPSCs, and LCLs, respectively.
source: Specifically 17.5%, 16.6%, and 16.8% of variance (median) in ASE was attributed to treatment effects in CMs, IPSCs, and LCLs, respectively, compared to 3.6%, 11.2%, and 21.9% variance (median) in total gene expression.
evidence: The manuscript reports this variance partitioning result.

claim: DEGs were characterized by high ASE compared to genes that do not respond to the treatments.
source: DEGs were characterized by high ASE compared to genes that do not respond to the treatments (Figure 5E).
evidence: The manuscript reports this comparison and references a figure.

claim: Genes associated with complex traits tend to have lower allelic expression.
source: Allelic expression was also elevated for genes tolerant to loss of function mutations, while genes associated with complex traits tend to have lower allelic expression (Figure 5F and G), which reflects the difference in phenotypic relevance for these gene categories.
evidence: The manuscript reports this observation and references figures.

claim: Genes with lower ratio of nonsynonymous to synonymous mutations (dN/dS, i.e. genes under negative selection) are associated with lower mean ASE.
source: Genes with lower ratio of nonsynonymous to synonymous mutations (dN/dS, i.e. genes under negative selection) are associated with lower mean ASE.
evidence: The manuscript reports this association.

claim: SNPs in genes with a TATA box had increased residual variance compared to SNPs in genes without a TATA box.
source: SNPs in genes with a TATA box had increased residual variance compared to SNPs in genes without a TATA box (Figure 5).
evidence: The manuscript reports this comparison and references a figure.

claim: GC content and CpG islands in a gene's promoter was associated with increased treatment variance and decreased residual variance.
source: In addition, GC content and CpG islands in a gene's promoter was associated with increased treatment variance and decreased residual variance.
evidence: The manuscript reports this association.

claim: Genes that are less tolerant to loss-of-function mutations and genes under negative selection (i.e. low dN/dS) have significantly lower residual variance.
source: As expected, genes that are less tolerant to loss-of-function mutations and genes under negative selection (i.e. low dN/dS) have significantly lower residual variance.
evidence: The manuscript reports this finding.

claim: Differential gene expression was associated with increased residual variance, suggesting that for genes with more dramatic responses to the environment, gene expression is under a less stringent genetic control.
source: When focusing on variance in allelic expression, we found differential gene expression to be associated with increased residual variance, suggesting that for genes with more dramatic responses to the environment, gene expression is under a less stringent genetic control (Figure 5E).
evidence: The manuscript reports this finding and provides an interpretation.

claim: Differentially spliced genes are associated with increased treatment variance, and not increased residual variance.
source: Differentially spliced genes, however, are associated with increased treatment variance, and not increased residual variance (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports this finding and references a figure.

claim: On average, half of the genes with dynamic regulatory interactions were missed by large eQTL mapping studies.
source: On average, half of the genes with dynamic regulatory interactions were missed by large eQTL mapping studies, indicating the importance of exploring multiple treatments to reveal previously unrecognized regulatory loci that may be important for disease.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding in the Abstract.

claim: Variation in environmental exposure can explain variation in gene expression in human population samples.
source: Variation in environmental exposure can explain variation in gene expression in human population samples (Gibson, 2008; Idaghdour et al., 2010; Favé et al., 2018; Aguirre-Gamboa et al., 2016; Horst et al., 2016; Maghbooli et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies supporting this claim.

claim: A highly correlated cluster of surfactant-related genes was found to be highly expressed in lung tissue from GTEx donors who died while on a ventilator.
source: For example, a highly correlated cluster of surfactant-related genes was found to be highly expressed in lung tissue from GTEx donors who died while on a ventilator (McCall et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study supporting this claim.

claim: Thousands of gene expression differences were identified between sun-exposed and non-sun-exposed skin.
source: Similarly, thousands of gene expression differences were identified between sun-exposed and non-sun-exposed skin (Kita and Fraser, 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study supporting this claim.

claim: Environmental exposures are able to alter splicing processes.
source: In addition to changing gene expression, environmental exposures are also able to alter splicing processes (Pai and Luca, 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study supporting this claim.

claim: The GTEx consortium observed a U-shaped pattern for eQTL tissue specificity, with eQTLs tending to be either highly shared amongst tissues or highly tissue-specific.
source: Specifically, the GTEx consortium observed a U-shaped pattern for eQTL tissue specificity, with eQTLs tending to be either highly shared amongst tissues or highly tissue-specific (The Gtex Consortium, 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites the GTEx consortium study supporting this claim.

claim: reQTL have been identified for infectious agents, drugs, and hormones, among other stimuli/perturbations.
source: reQTL have been identified for infectious agents, drugs, and hormones, among other stimuli/perturbations (Knowles et al., 2018; Manry et al., 2017; Nédélec et al., 2016; Alasoo et al., 2018; Kim-Hellmuth et al., 2017; Quach et al., 2016; Çalışkan et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2014; Fairfax et al., 2014; Maranville et al., 2011; Mangravite et al., 2013; Barreiro et al., 2012; Alasoo et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies supporting this claim.

claim: Studies have consistently shown that genes with G×E on gene expression are enriched for association with complex traits.
source: These studies have consistently shown that genes with G×E on gene expression are enriched for association with complex traits.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings from multiple cited studies.

claim: Nearly 50% of genes with cASE were involved in complex traits by GWAS, which is significantly greater than ASE or eQTL genes.
source: For example, nearly 50% of genes with cASE were involved in complex traits by GWAS, which is significantly greater than ASE or eQTL genes (Moyerbrailean et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study supporting this claim.

claim: Gene expression noise is gene-specific, dependent on promoter elements, and can be affected by genetic mutation.
source: This noise in gene expression is gene-specific, dependent on promoter elements, and can be affected by genetic mutation (Raser and O'Shea, 2004; Mogno et al., 2010), indicating its importance in gene regulation.
evidence: The manuscript cites studies supporting this claim.

claim: There has been selection to minimize gene expression noise in yeast.
source: Indeed, there has been selection to minimize gene expression noise in yeast (Lehner, 2008), and gene expression variation has been linked to differential gene expression in response to perturbation in flies and humans (Sigalova et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies supporting this claim.

claim: Gene expression variation has been linked to differential gene expression in response to perturbation in flies and humans.
source: Indeed, there has been selection to minimize gene expression noise in yeast (Lehner, 2008), and gene expression variation has been linked to differential gene expression in response to perturbation in flies and humans (Sigalova et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study supporting this claim.

claim: IPSC-derived CMs mimic primary CMs.
source: Extensive work by our group and others have shown that despite the potential introduction of reprogramming effects, IPSC-derived CMs mimic primary CMs (Pavlovic et al., 2018), recapitulate in vivo CM phenotypes (Matsa et al., 2016; Burridge et al., 2016; Carvajal-Vergara et al., 2010), retain donor-specific expression signatures (Panopoulos et al., 2017; Burrows et al., 2016; DeBoever et al., 2017; Rouhani et al., 2014), and can be used to assess the effects of environmental exposures on CM gene expression and cellular physiology (Ward and Gilad, 2019; Knowles et al., 2018; Sharma et al., 2017; Kitani et al., 2019; Matsa et al., 2016; Sharma et al., 2014; Burridge et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies supporting this claim.

claim: IPSC-derived CMs recapitulate in vivo CM phenotypes.
source: Extensive work by our group and others have shown that despite the potential introduction of reprogramming effects, IPSC-derived CMs mimic primary CMs (Pavlovic et al., 2018), recapitulate in vivo CM phenotypes (Matsa et al., 2016; Burridge et al., 2016; Carvajal-Vergara et al., 2010), retain donor-specific expression signatures (Panopoulos et al., 2017; Burrows et al., 2016; DeBoever et al., 2017; Rouhani et al., 2014), and can be used to assess the effects of environmental exposures on CM gene expression and cellular physiology (Ward and Gilad, 2019; Knowles et al., 2018; Sharma et al., 2017; Kitani et al., 2019; Matsa et al., 2016; Sharma et al., 2014; Burridge et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies supporting this claim.

claim: IPSC-derived CMs retain donor-specific expression signatures.
source: Extensive work by our group and others have shown that despite the potential introduction of reprogramming effects, IPSC-derived CMs mimic primary CMs (Pavlovic et al., 2018), recapitulate in vivo CM phenotypes (Matsa et al., 2016; Burridge et al., 2016; Carvajal-Vergara et al., 2010), retain donor-specific expression signatures (Panopoulos et al., 2017; Burrows et al., 2016; DeBoever et al., 2017; Rouhani et al., 2014), and can be used to assess the effects of environmental exposures on CM gene expression and cellular physiology (Ward and Gilad, 2019; Knowles et al., 2018; Sharma et al., 2017; Kitani et al., 2019; Matsa et al., 2016; Sharma et al., 2014; Burridge et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies supporting this claim.

claim: IPSC-derived CMs can be used to assess the effects of environmental exposures on CM gene expression and cellular physiology.
source: Extensive work by our group and others have shown that despite the potential introduction of reprogramming effects, IPSC-derived CMs mimic primary CMs (Pavlovic et al., 2018), recapitulate in vivo CM phenotypes (Matsa et al., 2016; Burridge et al., 2016; Carvajal-Vergara et al., 2010), retain donor-specific expression signatures (Panopoulos et al., 2017; Burrows et al., 2016; DeBoever et al., 2017; Rouhani et al., 2014), and can be used to assess the effects of environmental exposures on CM gene expression and cellular physiology (Ward and Gilad, 2019; Knowles et al., 2018; Sharma et al., 2017; Kitani et al., 2019; Matsa et al., 2016; Sharma et al., 2014; Burridge et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies supporting this claim.

claim: The heritability of heart failure is 26-34% based on pedigree analysis.
source: While pedigree analysis suggests that the heritability of heart failure is 26 - 34% (Lindgren et al., 2018), two recent, large-scale GWAS identified only eleven (Shah et al., 2020) and three (Arvanitis et al., 2020) genomic loci associated with heart failure.
evidence: The manuscript cites a study supporting this claim.

claim: Two recent, large-scale GWAS identified only eleven and three genomic loci associated with heart failure.
source: While pedigree analysis suggests that the heritability of heart failure is 26 - 34% (Lindgren et al., 2018), two recent, large-scale GWAS identified only eleven (Shah et al., 2020) and three (Arvanitis et al., 2020) genomic loci associated with heart failure.
evidence: The manuscript cites studies supporting this claim.

claim: Inflammation is a risk factor for atrial fibrillation.
source: Inflammation is a risk factor for atrial fibrillation (Hu et al., 2015; Harada et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies supporting this claim.

claim: In multiple population-based, case-control studies, corticosteroid use was associated with new-onset atrial fibrillation.
source: Additionally, in multiple population-based, case-control studies, corticosteroid use was associated with new-onset atrial fibrillation (Van Der Hooft et al., 2006; Christiansen et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies supporting this claim.

claim: Regulatory variation controlling the expression of Mendelian disease genes can affect complex trait risk.
source: While most causes of heart disease are not due to a mutation in a single gene, regulatory variation controlling the expression of Mendelian disease genes can affect complex trait risk (Freund et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study supporting this claim.

claim: Much of complex trait heritability is not explained by genome-wide significant variants, but rather results from the contribution of many variants with smaller effect sizes.
source: Much of complex trait heritability is not explained by genome-wide significant variants, but rather results from the contribution of many variants with smaller effect sizes (Manolio et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2010; Boyle et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies supporting this claim.

claim: Genes with a TATA box have increased noise in gene expression.
source: Prior work on gene expression variance has demonstrated that genes with a TATA box have increased noise (Mogno et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study supporting this claim.

claim: TATA box promoters have been associated with tissue-specific genes and high conservation across species.
source: TATA box promoters, as opposed to CpG island-associated promoters, have been associated with tissue-specific genes and high conservation across species (Carninci et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study supporting this claim.

claim: Mutations within splicing consensus sequences have catastrophic consequences in pre-mRNA splicing, eventually being associated with a plethora of different pathological conditions.
source: Mutations within these consensus sequences therefore have catastrophic consequences in pre-mRNA splicing, eventually being associated with a plethora of different pathological conditions (Faustino and Cooper, 2003; Lukong et al., 2008; Anna and Monika, 2018), including several forms of cystic fibrosis (Friedman et al., 1999; Bobadilla et al., 2002) and in both Becker and Duchenne muscular dystrophies (Habara et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies supporting this claim.

claim: Improper stop codon localization can activate the nonsense mRNA decay (NMD) pathway, resulting in transcript degradation.
source: These events have dramatic effects on RNA stability, as improper stop codon localization can activate the nonsense mRNA decay (NMD) pathway, resulting in transcript degradation (Brogna and Wen, 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study supporting this claim.

claim: Synonymous polymorphisms may alter the codon optimization of a given mRNA, a process which has been linked to reduced half-life.
source: Moreover, synonymous polymorphisms may alter the codon optimization of a given mRNA, a process which has been linked to reduced half-life (Presnyak et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study supporting this claim.

claim: Insulin itself is known to induce the expression of HIF1A.
source: Indeed, insulin itself is known to induce the expression of HIF1A (Treins et al., 2002), which we confirm in our differential gene expression data.
evidence: The manuscript cites a study and confirms the finding with their own data.

claim: The HIF pathway is especially important for cardiovascular disease and the response to cardiac ischemia.
source: In turn, the HIF pathway is especially important for cardiovascular disease and the response to cardiac ischemia (Semenza, 2014).
